title: They come, and they go
hookLine: a day that stings, then tilts back: Krishna's first teaching to a weeping Arjuna
carry: pleasure and pain pass; the self doesn't
tomorrow: what did the thunder say, three times?

lines: A DAY THAT STINGS, AND TILTS BACK.
cards: Arjuna is still in the chariot, eyes full of tears, grieving people who are standing right in front of him. And Krishna's first teaching isn't about war. It's about how things land.

Think of a day like that: a text that says can we talk, a grade lower than expected. Then a funny message, and the day tilts back. Krishna has a line for that tilting, and two core words sit in it: sukha and duhkha.

teach.b: Sukha: ease, happiness. Duhkha: pain, sorrow. Krishna calls Arjuna by his mother's name, Kaunteya, son of Kunti, and tells him: the touches of the senses bring cold and heat, pleasure and pain.
They come, and they go; they don't last. Bear them patiently. Nobody argues with weather, and nobody expects it to stay.
The word for them is agamapayinah: the coming-and-going ones. But why should anyone be able to stay steady? Krishna gives the reason one verse earlier.
The one who lives in this body passes through childhood, youth and old age, and on to another body, and the wise aren't confused by it.
That one is the atman, the self. Bodies change, feelings come and go; the self that lives through them doesn't. That's the big Hindu teaching under this verse.
Then: the steady person, the same in sukha and duhkha, whom these don't shake, is fit for the deathless.
A little later the Gita gives evenness a name: samatvam, and calls it yoga. Notice what it doesn't say.
It doesn't say the sting isn't real. Cold is cold, and a hard note from a teacher stings. It says the sting isn't you.
That's what Arjuna is offered: not numbness, but steadiness, from knowing what in him doesn't pass.

how: Hindus turn to Gita 2.13–15 in hard seasons and at times of loss: the self passes through childhood, youth and age, while pleasure and pain come and go.

s: the Gita says pain isn't real
it says pleasure and pain come and go; bear them patiently.
in Gita 2.13, the one who passes through childhood, youth and old age is the self, the atman
bodies and feelings change; the one who lives through them doesn't.
the steady person in the Gita feels nothing
the verse asks for steadiness in sukha and duhkha, not numbness.

games.q: your team loses the final after a great season. a teammate says, 'nothing matters anyway.' what fits Gita 2.14?
o: it stings, and it'll pass: the gita says pain comes and goes, and the self doesn't.
agree: steady people don't feel anything either way.
argue the last call until it finally feels fair.
games.why: the verse doesn't deny the sting. pleasure and pain come and go; the atman doesn't, so the steady one bears them without being shaken.

practice: Sit with the hands resting open on the knees or thighs, palms up. Let something from this week that stung rest in one hand, and something good in the other, and keep both hands equally still.
If the sting pulls one hand into a fist, open it again, gently. Notice who is watching both hands: the Gita says that one doesn't come and go. Let the breath come and go.

wordCard.voice: Two hundred core words, plain and returning. Today, sukha, ease, and duhkha, pain: a pair that comes and goes. And atman, the self, that doesn't.

orig.note: Sanskrit: ease and pain, the Gita's coming-and-going pair.

carryVoice: Pocket this: pleasure and pain pass; the self doesn't. Cold and heat, and the one who feels them. See you tomorrow.
